section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains the double language of "in the land of his father's sojournings, in the land of Canaan," interpreting Canaan as a merchant, analogous to the soul's descent for the sake of an ascent.
section.t: "And Yaakov settled in the land of his father's sojournings, in the land of Canaan,"
and our master, the Alter Rebbe, the master of redemption and joy, explains in his book Torah Ohr,
to understand the double language of "in the land of his father's sojournings, in the land of Canaan,"
that Canaan means a merchant,
as it is written,
"Canaanites, the honored of the land,"
and it is written,
"Canaan, in his hand are deceitful scales,"
and like a merchant who scatters money in order to profit and earn,
and his entire intention is to scatter and add more
[for the purpose of commerce is profit,
and as our sages, of blessed memory, said,
"Buy and sell, a merchant is called a trader"],
so too is the matter of the soul's descent below, that the purpose of the descent is for the sake of the ascent,
for specifically through its descent below and its enclothing in a body and the animal soul, it comes to a higher level than it was before its descent.

section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains Rashi's comment on the verse, questioning why the Torah records Esav's settlements briefly and Yaakov's at length, and clarifies that Esav's settlements are only recorded because they lead to Yaakov's.
section.t: And to understand this with more explanation and at greater length,
also to understand what Rashi said on the verse "And Yaakov settled,"
"After it wrote for you the settlements of Esav and his generations in a brief manner,
because they were not important and significant to elaborate, etc., it explained for you the settlements of Yaakov and his generations in a lengthy manner, etc."
For seemingly, since the settlements of Esav and his generations are not important and significant, there was no need to write them at all,
even not in a brief manner.
And it must be said,
that although the settlements of Esav,
in and of themselves,
are not important and significant,
nevertheless,
since through them one comes to the settlements of Yaakov,
Scripture wrote them.
However, because their entire significance is that through them one comes to the settlements of Yaakov,
it wrote them in a brief manner.
But not so the settlements of Yaakov and his generations,
which are important and significant in and of themselves,
it explained them in a lengthy manner.
And it is necessary to understand what is the matter of "through the settlements of Esav one comes to the settlements of Yaakov,"
and also it is necessary to understand the precise language of "a brief manner" and "a lengthy manner."
